summary: The Financial Times reported that OpenAI and Google provided AI model access to Singapore-based subsidiaries of Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent, whose parent companies were on a U.S. defence list. The reporting described the sales as legal under the rules then in force. The July account also reported that OpenAI had suspended several Alibaba-affiliated users in June over suspected model distillation. The reports do not identify a prohibited transfer through these subsidiaries or a materialised downstream harm from their access.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The reporting states that sales through the Singapore subsidiaries were legal under the rules then in force. Defence-list status of their parent companies therefore does not establish that a government access restriction applied to these transfers or was extended beyond its scope through service infrastructure. The separate June suspension over suspected distillation lacks the actor, conduct and rule facts needed for a mapping. The occurrence remains unclassified.

assessment_boundaries: Full original FT text and provider enforcement records remain unavailable; the directly reviewed secondary account contains attributed provider statements.
Incident admission does not determine legal liability or establish every disputed claim as final fact.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The occurrence relies principally on Financial Times reporting, which was not directly available for full-text review here, and on secondary accounts. The OECD.AI monitor records the transactions as legal and explicitly describes the situation as an AI hazard with no direct harm reported; its generated analysis is a cross-reference, not independent proof of a VIGIL failure. Suspicion of distillation and the reported June suspensions do not establish which entity performed restricted extraction, the scale of any extraction or a rule these reported sales violated. The directly reviewed July 10 secondary account places those suspensions in June. It does not establish when each reported service relationship began. Provider responses are quoted secondhand; original account and enforcement records are unavailable.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The evidence establishes reported lawful model-service sales to Singapore-based subsidiaries of listed Chinese parent firms and a separately reported June suspension of Alibaba-affiliated users over suspected distillation. It does not establish an export-control prohibition that the service provider propagated beyond its scope, nor identify the suspected extractor, verified extraction or the evidentiary basis of the suspension. The earlier Jurisdiction-Bounded Infrastructure Authority mapping treated a parent-company designation as though it were itself a service restriction; the class recognition conditions are not met on this record. Both clauses retain resolved-no-mapping dispositions. A listed parent is not itself an applicable model-service restriction, and lawful subsidiary sales do not prove circumvention or jurisdictional projection. Suspected extraction does not establish its actor, scale or legal violation. Independent external relevance review identifies no source-grounded canonical export-control or distillation rule for these reported lawful sales and suspected extraction. A parent-company designation does not identify a model-service prohibition. No canonical standards finding is admitted; this absence is not a compliance determination.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: CAM should distinguish a sovereign designation from a rule that actually governs model-service access, and distinguish a parent company from the subsidiary and users who receive service. Any future finding about restriction or circumvention would need the applicable rule, controlled actor, access route and attributable conduct.
